description.en-US: The sale this document is to be raised for. AN ORDER, not a bill, unlike sales_fiscal_request: the buyer's fiscal identity is agreed once for the sale, whatever it was settled in. Immutable, because re-pointing it would leave a snapshot the buyer confirmed attached to a sale they never saw. AT MOST ONE ACTIVE INSTRUCTION PER ORDER - cancelled ones are kept for audit, which is why the uniqueness is a partial index in the migration rather than a plain unique here.

The business partner the snapshot below was taken from. FOR TRACEABILITY ONLY: issuance reads the snapshot fields, never this reference, so a partner whose details changed after the buyer confirmed cannot silently alter what the document says. Nullable because an instruction may be filled in by hand before any partner is resolved.

The buyer's tax code AS CONFIRMED, not as the partner record holds it now. This is the field that makes the invoice deductible for a business buyer, and a document must say what the buyer agreed to at the time - a later correction to the partner is a new instruction, never a rewrite of this one.
The buyer's registered name as confirmed. Snapshotted for the same reason as tax_id: a company that renames itself does not thereby change the name on invoices it was already issued.
The address the document is made out to, as confirmed.

Where the issued document is sent. Unlike the other three this is often the buyer's own input rather than a copy of the partner record - the person at the till gives an address to receive it at, which need not be the company's registered one.

Where this instruction stands. Only 'ready' is picked up by the issuance job, so marking ready is the buyer's consent to be billed - an instruction still being filled in must never be issued from. 'processing' means a worker has claimed it and the snapshot is frozen. Declared no_update so a client cannot move it: every transition is an action that checks what it requires first.

Who created this instruction. Kept because the three carry different levels of assurance about the buyer's identity - a public self-service submission is the buyer's own claim, a back-office one was entered by staff - and a dispute over a wrong tax code turns on which it was.

Whether issuance should re-read the buyer from their party record instead of using the snapshot already captured. Set when the instruction is marked ready. It only matters on a second attempt: the first capture has nothing to reuse, whereas an instruction that came back from a failed issuance already holds a snapshot somebody reviewed, and refreshing it silently would change what is billed without anyone asking.

When the buyer's details were frozen onto this instruction, which happens once, immediately before it is locked for issuance. Empty until then: an unlocked instruction names a party rather than copying one.

When a worker claimed this instruction for issuance. Set as part of the same conditional write that moves it to 'processing', so claiming is atomic - two workers cannot both believe they own it, which is what would produce two documents for one sale.
When the buyer confirmed the information. Set on marking ready, and left alone by a later revert to draft: it records that consent was given, not that it is currently in force.
When the document came into existence, as reported by whoever issued it. Their date, not ours - a document bears the date its issuer gave it.
The issuer's own identifier for the document, and the only durable link to it. Written on confirmation and never regenerated: it is what a support enquiry or a reconciliation is traced through.
The issuer's code for the most recent failure, kept so an operator can tell a retryable outage from a rejection that needs the buyer's details corrected.
The most recent failure in the issuer's words. Only the latest is kept here; the full history is the attempt records.
